title: Mexico’s Secretary of Governance Announces Group of Experts Will Analyze National Registry of the Disappeared
author: Néstor Jiménez
content:
_This article by[Néstor
Jiménez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/N%C3%A9stor%20Jim%C3%A9nez)
originally appeared in the [October 14, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/14/politica/sg-anuncia-
que-grupo-de-expertos-realizara-analisis-del-registro-nacional-de-
desaparecidos), Mexico's premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. The Secretariat of Governance announced this Wednesday the
formation of a group of independent experts, both national and international,
who were contacted with the support of the Office of the United Nations High
Commissioner for Human Rights in Mexico. They will be responsible for carrying
out a “technical and scientific analysis” of the **national registry of
disappeared and missing persons** , detailed the head of this Secretariat,
Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez.

At a press conference, together with the Undersecretary of Human Rights,
Population and Migration, Arturo Medina, and the head of the National
Commission for the Search of Persons, Martha Lidia Pérez, the Secretary of
Governance stated that “their work will also make it possible to identify
possible legal and administrative improvements so that the national registry
fulfills the purpose established in the law: to be an effective tool for
search and location.”

At the same time, she announced that as a result of the ten pillars
established for the National Search Strategy, **16,003 people who had been
reported as disappeared have been located**.

It was detailed that 6,939 were located through the Single Identity Platform;
4,788 were the product of the strategy with the states; 3,473 through the
National Immediate Search Alert (ANBI), and 1,214 through searches in the
field.

From the ANBI command post, installed inside the headquarters of the
Secretariat of Governance, Rodríguez Velázquez recalled that one of the
commitments recently made by the federal government was the formation of a
group of national and international specialists.

Meanwhile, Undersecretary Medina noted that, with the support of the Office of
the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in Mexico, they held
meetings with national and international specialists in data analysis,
statistics, mathematics, artificial intelligence, and other disciplines, after
which they formed the working team.

He highlighted the participation of Mayank Kejriwal, a scientist at the
University of Southern California, specialist in artificial intelligence, and
complex systems.

Also joining will be Zubin Jelveh, a researcher at the University of Maryland,
expert in data analysis and public policy evaluation, as well as Ted
Enamorado, of the University of Washington, specialist in statistical and
probabilistic methods for linking records and integrating databases.

He announced that a data analysis specialist from Massachusetts will soon
join.

Likewise, Mexican specialists are joining this group, such as Astrid Adriana
Pozos, a researcher specializing in the disappearance of persons and human
identification, with experience at the International Committee of the Red
Cross; Esteban Salomón, a researcher at UNAM, specialist in the functioning of
prosecutors’ offices and the justice system; as well as Ernesto Insunza Vera,
a researcher at the Center for Research and Higher Studies in Social
Anthropology (CIESAS) in Veracruz, who is an expert in accountability and
citizen participation.

At the same time, Guillermo Guevara, a specialist in security and justice
public policy, is participating, as well as Rodrigo Canales, a professor at
Boston University, expert in institutional strengthening, public security, and
violence reduction.

“This group brings together knowledge in artificial intelligence, statistics,
data analysis, public policy, justice systems, disappearance of persons, and
institutional strengthening. It is a technical group that is going to help us
from a specialized and scientific perspective in several tasks.”

> We want them to audit us, we want them to review us, we want all the
> information to be transparent, and that is why today we are pleased to be
> able to announce that this team of national and international experts has
> now been formed.
>
> Arturo Medina, Undersecretary of Human Rights

He underlined that they asked them for **three fundamental tasks** : to review
and technically validate the methodologies being used, in order to analyze the
national registry with objectivity, and from technical and scientific
knowledge.

They entrusted them with establishing differentiated criteria, based on
international practices, for the records that have sufficient information to
carry out a search, and to detect those that require their data to be
completed and those in which activity has been identified after the date of
disappearance.

They must define the treatment to be given to the records that, according to
the analysis that has been carried out, do not have complete or sufficient
information to identify a person or to carry out a search for them.

As a third task, they were asked to propose better techniques, technical
improvements, and, when necessary, legal or administrative reforms that make
it possible to maintain a reliable, up-to-date registry that is an effective
tool for the search for disappeared and missing persons.
